La convolución de dos señales mezcla una: The convolution of two signals mixes one with the other: $y(t) = (x * h)(t) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ$. For each instant $t$, $h$ is flipped, moved to $t$ and the area of its product with $x$ is measured. That is what the graph above animates.
Si $x(t)$ es la entrada de un sistema li: If $x(t)$ is the input of a linear time-invariant system (a circuit of resistors, capacitors and inductors is one) and $h(t)$ its impulse response, the output is exactly $y = x * h$: each instant of the input is a small impulse, the system responds to each with $h$ and the output is the sum of all those responses.
Es conmutativa, $x * h = h * x$, así que: It is commutative, $x * h = h * x$, so it does not matter which of the two is flipped. The duration of $y$ is the sum of the durations, and its area is the product of the areas: $∫ y = (∫ x)(∫ h)$. With an impulse it is shifted without change: $x(t) * δ(t − a) = x(t − a)$. A pure delay is then a delayed impulse.
Si la entrada es el escalón $u(t)$, la s: If the input is the step $u(t)$, the output is the integral of the impulse response: $s(t) = ∫_{0}^{t} h(τ) dτ$, and conversely, $h(t) = ds/dt$. From $s(t)$ come the data measured in the lab: the rise time (from 10 % to 90 % of the final value), the overshoot (how far it goes past) and the settling time (when it stays within 2 % of the final value).
Un filtro RC paso bajo tiene $τ = R C$,: A low-pass RC filter has $τ = R C$, $h(t) = {1}/{τ} e^{−t/τ} u(t)$ and $s(t) = 1 − e^{−t/τ}$: it never overshoots and takes $2.2 τ$ to rise from 10 % to 90 %. A series RLC (with the output across the capacitor) has $ω_0 = 1/√(L C)$ and $ζ = {R}/{2} √(C/L)$. If $ζ < 1$ it oscillates as it rises and overshoots by $e^{−πζ/√(1 − ζ^2)}$ of the final value; with $ζ = 1$ it is the fastest response without overshoot; with $ζ > 1$ it is slow but does not oscillate.
Un RL con la salida en la resistencia es: An RL with the output across the resistor is a low-pass with $τ = L/R$. If the output is taken across the resistor of an RC, the filter is a high-pass: $H(s) = sτ/(1 + sτ)$ and $h(t) = δ(t) − {1}/{τ} e^{−t/τ} u(t)$, with area 0 because it blocks DC; the step response starts at 1 and dies away as $e^{−t/τ}$. The RLC with the output across the resistor is a band-pass: $H(s) = 2ζω_0 s/(s^2 + 2ζω_0 s + ω_0^2)$, also with area 0 (it does not pass DC) and with its maximum response near $ω_0$.
Con señales muestreadas la integral pasa: With sampled signals the integral becomes a sum: $y[n] = ∑_k x[k]\,h[n − k]$. If $x$ has $N$ values and $h$ has $M$, $y$ has $N + M − 1$ and starts at the sum of the initial indices; the sum of $y$ is the product of the sums. It is also polynomial multiplication: the coefficients of $(1 + 2z + 3z^2)(1 + z)$ are $\{1, 3, 5, 3\}$. The three-sample moving average is the convolution with $\{1/3, 1/3, 1/3\}$.
Los tiempos van en segundos y admiten pr: Times are in seconds and accept prefixes: 2m or 2 ms are two milliseconds, 10µ ten microseconds. Components too: 4k7 is 4.7 kΩ, 100n is 100 nF. The decimal comma is accepted. In two-signal mode the numbers need not be seconds: it works for any unit.
